drills.q: Given width:200px, padding:20px, border:5px, compute the final rendered width under content-box and under border-box.
drills.a: content-box: 250px total (200 content + 40px padding both sides + 10px border both sides, all added on top of the declared width). border-box: exactly 200px total -- the content area shrinks to 150px to make room for padding and border within the declared width.

drills.q: State the decision rule for choosing Flexbox vs Grid for a given layout, beyond '1D vs 2D.'
drills.a: Ask whether items need to align across both rows and columns simultaneously as a structural requirement (page shells, card grids that must line up row-to-row, aligned form fields) -- use Grid. If distributing/aligning along a single row or column with wrapping as a secondary concern -- use Flexbox. They compose: Grid for outer structure, Flexbox for alignment within individual grid items is a normal, common pattern.

drills.q: Why doesn't z-index:9999 bring an element above a sibling with z-index:1, and what's the actual debugging method?
drills.a: z-index only compares elements within the same stacking context -- if the high z-index element is nested inside an ancestor that itself created a new stacking context (opacity<1, transform, filter, position:fixed/sticky, will-change, isolation:isolate, or position:relative/absolute with non-auto z-index), its z-index has no meaning relative to anything outside that context. Debug by tracing ancestors for stacking-context-creating properties (DevTools Layers panel or computed styles), not by raising the number.

drills.q: List every property/condition that creates a new stacking context.
drills.a: position:fixed or sticky (unconditionally); position:relative/absolute combined with a non-auto z-index; opacity less than 1; transform other than none; filter/backdrop-filter other than none; will-change naming a stacking-context-triggering property; isolation:isolate; being a flex/grid item with a non-auto z-index.

drills.q: A position:fixed modal overlay scrolls away with the page instead of staying pinned to the viewport. Diagnose.
drills.a: Check ancestors for transform, filter, will-change:transform, perspective, or contain:layout -- any of these establishes a new containing block for fixed descendants, overriding the expected viewport-relative behavior, so the 'fixed' element becomes positioned relative to that ancestor and scrolls when it scrolls. Fix: remove the property from the ancestor, or portal the modal to document.body.

drills.q: Explain margin collapsing with concrete numbers, and why Flexbox/Grid children avoid it.
drills.a: Adjacent vertical margins between block-level siblings in normal flow collapse to the larger value, not the sum -- margin-bottom:20px followed by margin-top:30px produces a 30px gap total, not 50px. This is vertical-only, normal-flow-only behavior; Flexbox and Grid items don't participate in margin collapsing at all, which is why gap on a flex/grid container is more predictable than margin-based spacing.

drills.q: A card component must switch to a side-by-side internal layout once it has at least 400px of available width, and it's used in both a wide dashboard and a narrow sidebar. Design the CSS, and explain why media queries can't solve this.
drills.a: container-type:inline-size on the card's wrapper, then @container (min-width:400px) { .card { grid-template-columns: ...; } } on its internal layout -- responds to the actual container width regardless of viewport. Media queries only see viewport width, so they can't distinguish 'this component happens to be in a narrow sidebar' from 'the viewport itself is narrow' -- structurally the wrong signal for a reusable component.

drills.q: What are logical properties, why do they matter beyond RTL support, and what's the tradeoff of adopting them?
drills.a: Logical properties (margin-inline-start, padding-block-end, inset-inline-start) express spacing/positioning in flow-relative terms rather than fixed physical directions -- inline-start maps to left in LTR horizontal writing but auto-flips for RTL and reorients for vertical writing modes, eliminating the need for a parallel RTL override stylesheet. Tradeoff: no real performance cost, but genuine unfamiliarity/readability friction for teams used to physical properties.

drills.q: What does isolation:isolate do, when is it a deliberate fix rather than a workaround, and what's its risk if overused?
drills.a: It forces a new stacking context without any other side-effecting property (no forced opacity/transform), used deliberately to sandbox a self-contained component's internal z-index values so they can't leak out and conflict with the rest of the page. Risk: it can trap content that legitimately needs to stack above something outside its own subtree (e.g., a tooltip that must render above a sibling modal), recreating the exact stacking-boundary problem it was meant to solve, just self-inflicted.

drills.q: Before container queries, how did teams solve the 'component must adapt to its actual container width, not the viewport' problem, and what did that cost?
drills.a: ResizeObserver in JavaScript, watching the container element and toggling a class or inline style based on measured width. It worked but added JS runtime cost, a layout-thrashing risk if reads/writes weren't batched carefully, and an extra render-cycle lag -- all of which pure CSS container queries (full browser support as of 2026) eliminate entirely.
